Figure 4.16: Export System Page70 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version Figure 4.17: Typical CO Berth Arrangement 2 4.5.6 CO TRAIN & TRUCK RECEIVING STATIONS 2 There are three CO unloading stations available which can service both rail and truck transport. Each 2 station is equipped with a loading arm package that includes an LCO unloading arm, a CO vapor return 2 2 arm, and one spare arm capable of either service. The loading arms have a 20-meter reach radius which can access up to four rail cars when parked on site. Additionally, there are four onloading pumps, of which three are operational and one serves as a spare. There are two metering packages equipped with an analyzer (ref. 4.5.4 Metering Analyzer Packages). The loading arm packages will have to be elevated to maximize the reach over top of the rail car areas. Elevation of the loading arms will be reviewed further during FEED to assess whether site grading and/or elevated structure support is required or preferred. The four onloading pumps are positioned close to the loading arm area to maximize available suction head and reduce liquid drop out. The metering packages will be located just east of the loading pump area prior to entering the pipe rack system. See Fig. 4.18 which highlights the various CO train and truck receiving equipment components. 2 Page71 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version Figure 4.18: Train & Truck Receiving Stations 4.5.7 CO VENT STACK 2 A 50-meter-high vent stack has been positioned on the north side of the facility, just east of the liquefaction train area. Currently, a 30-meter radius exclusion zone surrounds the vent stack, ensuring no plant equipment is within this area to prevent personnel from entering. It is anticipated that the height and exclusion zone will likely decrease once additional dispersion analysis is completed during the FEED phase. For now, the height and restriction zone are considered a conservative worst-case requirement (see Fig. 4.19). The vent stack at its current height may pose a challenge to Peter O Knight Airport, which is 1.5 miles away, and MacDill Air Force Base, about 5 miles away. Port Tampa Bay engineers believe it will eventually be approved. Nonetheless, efforts will be made to reduce its height in the FEED stage.
